title: A fixed-density transit correction leaves a 6 to 12 hour peak in 4,091 TESS rapid rotators
abstract: We test whether transit geometry explains the period dependence of complex periodic variable (CPV) detections in a released TESS sample. There are 126 clear on-target labels among 4,091 rapid rotators from sectors 56 to 107. At fixed stellar density, a small cloud at corotation has crossing probability proportional to period to the power -2/3. An exact log-binomial model uses this factor and adjusts for color and height above the main sequence. Relative to 6 to 12 hours, the corrected detection ratio is 0.382 (95% interval 0.195 to 0.747) below 6 hours, 0.546 (0.380 to 0.785) at 12 to 24 hours, and 0.084 (0.034 to 0.209) at 24 to 48 hours. The long-period deficit remains in source and data-quality subsets. A bounded logistic sensitivity model adds observation controls and gives the same direction. Thus the specified geometry alone does not fit these detections. Inclination selection, uncertain density, cloud geometry and unmeasured detection efficiency can change the physical interpretation. We measure a window in detected morphology, not intrinsic occurrence or material survival. Original code, aggregate evidence, source hashes and separate-scratch repeat steps are included; external record tables are excluded.
